analysis.one_liner: Removes Medicare's limits on what physicians can charge seniors directly.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsor and died in the Senate Finance Committee at the end of the 101st Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the rules that cap what doctors can charge Medicare patients above Medicare's approved payment amounts, and would erase the distinction between doctors who agree to accept Medicare rates and those who do not. Starting in 1990, doctors could bill Medicare patients for any amount beyond Medicare's payment. The bill was introduced by Senator Symms in January 1989 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians, who would no longer be bound by Medicare's limits on charges. Doctors who did not accept Medicare's approved rates could charge elderly and disabled patients any amount above what Medicare paid, with no cap.

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the 'reasonable charge' limit that tied what Medicare pays to the physician's own full charge for participating doctors, and repeals the actual-charge limits in section 1842(j), (l), and (m) of the Social Security Act.

Ends the participation-agreement structure and directs the Secretary, for services on or after January 1, 1990, to determine payment 'without regard to whether the physician was a participating or nonparticipating physician in any previous year,' effectively erasing the distinction between the two categories.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries, mostly seniors and people with disabilities, who would face unlimited out-of-pocket charges from doctors billing above Medicare's approved amounts, and Medicare itself, which could pay more for physician services without charge limits.

drawbacks.text: Removing charge limits means doctors could bill Medicare patients unlimited amounts above Medicare's payment, raising out-of-pocket costs for seniors and disabled beneficiaries with no ceiling.

Eliminating the participating-physician distinction removes the financial incentive for doctors to accept Medicare's approved rates as payment in full, undermining a long-standing cost-control structure for the Medicare program.

A good-faith argument for relaxing charge limits is that doctors who feel underpaid may refuse to treat Medicare patients or accept Medicare assignment; the bill's approach, however, addressed that by shifting the cost to patients rather than adjusting Medicare's payment rates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded away the main protection seniors have against excess doctor billing — the limits on charges above Medicare's approved amounts — in exchange for the possibility that more doctors would be willing to treat Medicare patients. The costs fall directly on elderly and disabled patients through unlimited balance billing, and the bill offered no mechanism to raise Medicare's payment rates instead, so the burden of the change fell on the people least able to bear it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in January 1989 and never got a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Symms introduced the bill on January 25, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was recorded; the bill died in committee when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries kept the existing caps on what doctors can charge them, and physicians did not get the unlimited billing rights the bill would have granted.

for.name: Sen. Steven D. Symms
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to eliminate Medicare's limits on physician charges.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or vote for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Lloyd Bentsen
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no recorded votes, so no party split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have freed doctors from Medicare's caps on charges, letting them bill elderly and disabled patients unlimited amounts above Medicare's payment. Doctors' gain would have come directly out of patients' pockets.
Beneficiaries would have lost protection against excess billing, and Medicare's cost controls over physician fees would have been dismantled.
